content.text: Write a 500-word essay about the history of the ls command. No tools.
I will write a 500-word essay on the history of the ls command without using any tools.

The `ls` command is one of the oldest and most familiar tools in the Unix tradition. Its name is an abbreviation of “list,” and its job has always been simple: show the names of files in a directory. That simplicity is why it survived more than fifty years of operating-system change.

Unix began at Bell Labs around 1969. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie built a small system for the PDP-7, then the PDP-11, and they needed a way to inspect directories from the shell. Early Unix already had a program that listed directory entries. By the time the first edition of the Unix Programmer’s Manual appeared in 1971, `ls` was documented as a standard command. The first versions printed names in a single column. Options arrived quickly. Users wanted hidden files, long listings with permissions and sizes, and output sorted by time.
